analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and health insurers to publish their real prices and negotiated rates so patients can see costs in advance.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: after introduction it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in January 2023 and received no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Public Health Service Act and the Affordable Care Act to force hospitals to publish, in plain language and machine-readable form, their gross charges, the rates they negotiated with each insurer, their discounted cash prices, and billing codes for at least 300 common schedulable services. Health insurance plans would have to publish in-network and out-of-network rates and negotiated prescription-drug prices, and provide a free online tool so patients could look up what a specific service would cost them before getting it. Hospitals that refused would face a civil penalty of up to $300 per day of ongoing violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and families shopping for scheduled hospital care, imaging, lab work, or prescriptions gain the ability to see, before treatment, what a hospital charges insurers and what a plan will actually cover — enabling price comparison and helping the roughly one-third of Americans who face surprise medical bills or pay cash for care. Employers and unions that buy coverage also gain, because the bill extends disclosure to self-insured group plans, exposing the rates insurers and hospitals charge them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients facing hospital and drug bills

how_it_helps.text: Requires every hospital to publish, free and in machine-readable form, its gross charges, the rates it negotiated with each insurer, its minimum and maximum negotiated rates, its discounted cash price, and billing codes — so patients can compare prices before scheduling care.

Requires hospitals to publish standard charges for at least 300 schedulable 'shoppable' services, or to maintain a free, publicly accessible online price-estimator tool that gives a real-time estimate of what the patient will owe.

Requires health insurance plans to publish in-network and out-of-network rates and the negotiated rates for prescription drugs, and to provide a searchable online tool plus on-request paper disclosures showing an individual's estimated out-of-pocket cost for a specific service.
Extends the insurer disclosure requirements beyond Obamacare marketplace plans to essentially all group and individual health coverage, including self-insured employer plans.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health insurers bear compliance costs to publish hundreds of services' negotiated rates and maintain consumer-facing price tools, plus a commercial cost: once negotiated rates are public, hospitals lose the ability to keep confidential discounts and charge uninsured or cash-paying patients more. PBMs and drug intermediaries face exposure of the rebate-derived net prices on prescription drugs.

drawbacks.text: The civil monetary penalty for a hospital that refuses to disclose its prices is capped at $300 per day of ongoing violation — a few hundred dollars a day against hospitals with billion-dollar budgets, which the bill's own sponsors' framework leaves weak as an enforcement stick.

Most of what the bill requires — hospital standard-charge disclosure and insurer cost-sharing tools — largely mirrors federal transparency rules already issued administratively, so a main practical effect is to harden existing rules into statute rather than add new disclosure.

Hospitals and insurers face real compliance costs to publish machine-readable files for hundreds of shoppable services and maintain real-time estimator tools, and there is an honest concern among providers that publicly exposing negotiated rates could push some prices upward rather than down.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — real price information for patients before they receive care — is genuine, and price opacity is a large part of why hospital and drug costs are unpredictable for working families. The drawbacks are real too: the bill's $300-a-day penalty cap is too small to force a large hospital system to comply, the bill largely makes permanent rules that already exist administratively (so its incremental effect depends on enforcement the bill barely funds), and publishing negotiated rates could push some low-discount hospitals' prices upward. On balance it is a consumer-friendly bill, but a weakly enforced one. Its clearest cost was that it never moved at all: patients got no new statutory protection from it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 20, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
One week later, on January 27, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the 118th Congress.
It attracted only two cosponsors, both House Republicans, and no committee vote or floor vote ever occurred.

The bill's substance — hospital standard-charge disclosure and insurer cost-transparency tools — largely tracks federal transparency rules already in effect administratively, so the practical loss from the bill's death was the loss of statutory permanence and its modest added requirements, not the removal of an existing safeguard.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and health insurers are better off, because the negotiated rates and cash prices the bill would have forced into the open stayed out of statutory law, and the existing transparency rules remain enforcement-poor and administratively reversible rather than locked in by Congress.

for.name: Rep. Warren Davidson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write hospital and insurer price-disclosure requirements into statute.

for.name: 2 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it attracted no Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee: after its January 2023 referral, no hearing, markup, or committee vote was scheduled during the entire Congress.

against.name: Hospital industry groups (e.g., the American Hospital Association)
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed making detailed negotiated-rate disclosure mandatory and enforceable, arguing it exposes confidential contracts; their lobbying against enforceable price transparency is well documented.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a recorded vote; it was a Republican-sponsored effort with two Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support, but no party bloc ever had to vote on it because it never left the Health Subcommittee.

industries.note: The bill forces hospitals to publish the discounted rates they negotiate with every insurer and their cash prices, exposing the spread between list prices and what insurers actually pay and undercutting hospitals' ability to charge uninsured patients more. Its interest runs against price-shopping patients.

Insurers would have to publish in-network and out-of-network rates for all plans and build consumer cost-estimator tools. Because they already operate under similar federal disclosure rules, the incremental loss is smaller than hospitals', but disclosure erodes the information advantage behind network pricing.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug intermediaries
industries.note: Plans must disclose negotiated prescription-drug rates and historical net prices inclusive of rebates, shining light on the opaque rebate chain between drugmakers, PBMs, and insurers. It would not directly cap drug prices, so the effect is disclosure pressure rather than an immediate revenue hit.
